newsitem.title: USA: Struggle for Miami could raise racial tension.
newsitem.headline: Struggle for Miami could raise racial tension.

text.p: The struggle to revoke the city of Miami's charter and have its government absorbed by Dade County could expose raw nerves in the city's ethnic communities before a vote this year, analysts say.
Officials certified on Tuesday that petitions calling for the abolition of the city government had enough signatures to force a vote. The election must be held within 240 days.

Backers of the referendum are ready to write an epitaph for Florida's leading city, whose name has long been synonymous with sunshine, palm trees, white sand beaches and a Latin flavor, saying Miami is hopelessly corrupt.
Mayor Joe Carollo feels otherwise, vowing "I will not let the demise of the city of Miami happen, not on my watch."

The drive to abolish the government capped a miserable Centennial year in which three city officials, including the city manager, were indicted for corruption. Their downfall revealed the city was facing a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct. 1. It is now under the supervision of a state oversight board.

One of 29 cities making up the metropolitan area that sprawls across Dade County, Miami includes crime-ridden, rundown areas such as Liberty City and Overtown, and Little Havana, with its Cuban restaurants, clubs and shops, where many Cuban refugees have arrived penniless and made good.

Petition campaign leader Gene Stearns says Miami, with large areas that are slums dependent on tax money from a few rich parts such as downtown and Coconut Grove, is too broke to provide services from crime prevention to trash collection
"There aren't enough people to carry the burden and the burden must be spread," Stearns, a lawyer, said.

Asked about the implications for Miami's blacks if the city disappeared, he said: "The city has a sad history of segregation and ignoring blighted black areas. The only way we are going to improve government in an area like Liberty City is to ask other areas to contribute."
But Lloyd Major, director of community relations at the Office of Black Affairs, said blacks expected little to change for them whatever happened to the city.

"My hope is that city will not be abolished. It would be a mark and a stain that would take a long time to remove," he told Reuters. "I don't think it would be good thing, but it would not necessarily have a negative impact (on blacks)."
Major said many blacks were simply not in Miami's economic mainstream and that many blamed Cuban Americans who had gained power in Miami for the mess it was in.

In elections in November forced by the corruption scandal, blacks lost their only seat on the city commission to Cuban American Humberto Hernandez, who has visited Spanish language radio stations in recent days to broadcast appeals against abolishing Miami's government. Mayor Carollo is also of Cuban descent.

Most of the Cuban community, part of a Hispanic population that is now the dominant ethnic group in Miami, was likely to resist abolition, Milan Dluhy, an economics professor at the Florida International University, said.
"The Cubans have just got power. They will say 'Now you want to take it away from us,'" he said. "A lot of people among the Cuban community identify with Miami.

"It looks like its going to be an ethnic struggle," Dluhy said, although he argued that blacks, who are better represented and have more public employment opportunities in the county goverment than in Miami, may benefit from a change.
Jerry Haar of the University of Miami's North-South Center said abolition of Miami was not a question of jurisdiction but about quality of services.

"This is the northernmost banana republic in the hemisphere," he said. "The city has failed to attract business that could create jobs. The schools stink, the roads stink. Whether you live in Coconut Grove or Liberty City, you're going to be unhappy."
